Breadth means width — the measurement of how far something extends from one side to the other. If you measure a swimming pool and find it stretches 10 meters from the left wall to the right wall, that 10 meters is its breadth.

However — and this is crucial — the word is far more commonly used in a figurative sense to describe the wide scope, range, or variety of something non-physical, like knowledge, experience, or topics. This figurative use is where the word truly lives in modern language.

In its literal sense, breadth simply means width. It answers the question: how wide is this?

"The breadth of the river made it impossible to cross on foot." Here, breadth tells you the river is too wide to walk across.

"The workers measured the breadth of the tunnel before ordering the equipment." They need to know how wide it is.

In this physical sense, breadth and width mean essentially the same thing. The difference is mostly tone — breadth sounds a little more formal and literary, while width is the everyday word. You'd say "the width of this table" in casual conversation, but "the breadth of the valley" in a novel.

Now imagine you are standing at the edge of a vast open field and you look from left to right. The field stretches wide before you. That image — something spreading out widely, covering a lot of ground — is exactly what breadth captures when applied to ideas, knowledge, and subjects.

When used figuratively, breadth describes how much something covers, how many different areas or things it includes, and how wide its reach is.

"The breadth of her knowledge is remarkable — she can discuss medicine, philosophy, architecture, and music with equal confidence." This means she knows about many different subjects. Her knowledge doesn't just go in one direction; it spreads wide.

"The report examined the full breadth of the company's problems." This means the report looked at all the different kinds of problems — not just one or two, but the entire wide range of them.

"He was hired for the breadth of his experience." He has worked in many different fields or roles, and that variety is what makes him valuable.

In each of these cases, breadth is about how many different things are covered or included, not about how deeply any one of them is explored.
Breadth vs. Depth — The Most Important Contrast

The single best way to lock in the figurative meaning of breadth is to understand how it contrasts with depth.

Breadth is about how wide — how many different areas, topics, or kinds of things are covered.
Depth is about how deep — how thoroughly, carefully, or profoundly any one area is explored.

Picture a person who has read fifty books, each on a completely different subject — cooking, astronomy, history, poetry, economics, biology. That person has breadth of reading. They have touched many different fields.

Now picture a person who has spent their entire life reading every single book ever written about astronomy — every journal, every textbook, every research paper. That person has extraordinary depth in astronomy, but their reading might lack breadth in other areas.

This contrast is everywhere in real life:

"The university course gives students breadth across many subjects, but doesn't go into great depth in any single one."

"A good doctor needs both breadth — knowing about many different conditions — and depth — knowing each condition thoroughly."

"His speech impressed the audience with its breadth of ideas, but critics felt it lacked depth."

There is often an undertone of admiration when someone uses the word breadth. When a person says "I was struck by the breadth of her work," they are not neutrally stating that it covered many topics — they are implying that the range was remarkably wide, wide enough to be noteworthy.

This makes breadth slightly different from just saying "many" or "various." It carries a quiet suggestion that the scope is genuinely impressive or substantial.

"The breadth of something" is the most standard construction: the breadth of knowledge, the breadth of experience, the breadth of the problem, the breadth of support. It simply means the full, wide range of that thing.

"The full breadth of something" emphasizes that you are considering all of it, not just a part: "We must understand the full breadth of this crisis before we act." Nothing is being left out.

"Breadth of vision" means the ability to think widely and consider many different possibilities, perspectives, or ideas. A leader with breadth of vision can see the big picture and think beyond narrow or obvious solutions.

"A hair's breadth" is a very common idiom meaning an extremely tiny distance or margin — barely any space at all. "Breadth" here refers to the width of a single strand of hair, which is almost nothing.

"She escaped the falling tree by a hair's breadth." She barely got away — by almost no margin at all.
"The election was decided by a hair's breadth." The winning margin was incredibly small.

This phrase is used whenever you want to express that something was just barely avoided or achieved.

Breadth, as a noun, has two closely connected meanings that share the same underlying idea of wideness. Literally, it is the physical measurement of width — how far something extends from one side to the other. Figuratively — and far more commonly — it describes the wide range, scope, and variety of something non-physical, such as knowledge, experience, or topics covered. The wider the range, the greater the breadth. Its natural opposite is depth, which is about how thoroughly something is explored rather than how much ground it covers. And in the idiom "a hair's breadth," it shrinks to mean the tiniest possible margin.
